nameStory: The 'downy' in downy hawthorn comes from the soft, fuzzy hairs that cover the undersides of its leaves and young twigs, giving them a velvety texture when you run your fingers along them. This downy coating helps distinguish it from many of its smooth-leaved hawthorn cousins. Like all hawthorns, it gets the 'haw' part of its name from the Old English word for hedge, since these thorny trees were traditionally planted as living fences.
description: Downy hawthorn is a small to medium-sized tree that typically grows 15-25 feet tall with a rounded, spreading crown. It belongs to the rose family and shows this heritage through its clusters of white, five-petaled flowers in spring and small red fruits in fall. The tree is armed with sharp thorns along its branches and has distinctively soft, fuzzy leaves that feel almost velvety to the touch. In New England, it's quite rare, making any sighting a special discovery.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are broadly oval with shallow lobes and feel noticeably soft and fuzzy underneath due to dense downy hairs - run your finger along the underside for the distinctive velvety texture that gives this tree its name

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: White flowers appear in flat-topped clusters in late spring, each flower having 5 rounded petals and numerous stamens with pink or red anthers, creating a delicate lacy appearance

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red berries about half an inch across ripen in late summer, each containing several hard seeds and having a sweet-tart taste with mealy texture

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Gray to brown bark becomes scaly with age, peeling off in small plates to reveal lighter patches underneath, creating a mottled appearance on older trunks

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a small tree with an open, rounded crown and branches armed with sharp thorns up to 2 inches long - watch your hands when examining closely

habitat: In New England, downy hawthorn prefers rich, moist soils in woodland edges, stream valleys, and bottomlands where it can get partial sun. Look for it along the borders between forests and open areas, or in clearings within deciduous woodlands. It thrives in areas with good drainage but consistent moisture, often growing alongside other members of the rose family like wild cherries and serviceberries.

seasonality.spring: White flower clusters bloom in May, filling the air with a sweet fragrance that attracts bees and other pollinators. New leaves emerge with a bronze tint before turning green, their downy coating most noticeable on young foliage.
seasonality.summer: Leaves are fully developed and deep green, with the fuzzy underside texture at its most pronounced. Small green fruits begin developing after flowers fade.
seasonality.fall: Bright red berries ripen and become conspicuous against yellowing foliage. Leaves may turn yellow to orange before dropping, and fruits often persist after leaf fall.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the thorny structure and scaly bark pattern. Some fruits may remain on branches, and the overall branching pattern shows the characteristic spreading crown shape.

funFact: Despite being armed with fierce thorns, downy hawthorn fruits were traditionally made into jellies and wines, and the flowers were once commonly used to make a fragrant tea believed to strengthen the heart - in fact, hawthorn extracts are still used in modern herbal medicine for heart health.
confusionNotes: With over 20 hawthorn species in New England, identification can be tricky! The key to downy hawthorn is right in the name - run your finger under the leaves for that distinctive soft, velvety feeling. Most other hawthorns have smooth or only slightly hairy leaves that lack this pronounced downy texture.
contextualKnowledge: Hawthorns are notoriously difficult to identify even for botanists, with many species hybridizing freely and showing variable characteristics. The genus Crataegus is considered one of the most challenging groups in North American botany, so don't feel discouraged if hawthorn identification seems overwhelming at first!
compareHints: Among New England's many hawthorns, downy hawthorn stands out for its distinctly fuzzy leaf undersides - most others like dotted hawthorn or common hawthorn have smooth or only slightly hairy leaves. The soft, velvety texture is so pronounced you can feel it immediately when you touch the leaf underside, unlike the subtle hairiness of species like cockspur hawthorn. Its larger leaves and red fruits also help separate it from the smaller-leaved Washington hawthorn.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Dotted hawthorn stands out from its many New England relatives primarily by its spotted fruits.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, common hawthorn stands out for having just one seed per fruit (most others have 2-5 seeds) and deeply lobed leaves with 3-7 divisions.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, cockspur stands out with the longest thorns - much longer than dotted hawthorn's short spines or Washington hawthorn's modest thorns.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, big-fruit hawthorn stands out for its notably larger berries and earlier bloom time.
Among New England hawthorns, large-thorn hawthorn stands out primarily for its exceptionally long, straight thorns that dwarf those of relatives like dotted hawthorn or common hawthorn.

Among the many hawthorn species in New England, Washington hawthorn stands out with its distinctly triangular, deeply lobed leaves (rather than the more oval or rounded leaves of species like dotted hawthorn).
Among New England's many hawthorn species, waxy-fruited hawthorn stands out primarily for its distinctively coated berries - no other local hawthorn has that waxy, frosted appearance on the fruits.

Among New England's many hawthorns, fireberry hawthorn stands out for its golden-yellow unripe fruits - most relatives like dotted hawthorn or cockspur hawthorn have green unripe fruits that turn red.
Large-flowered cockspurthorn stands out from its many hawthorn relatives primarily by its notably large flowers - nearly twice the size of most other hawthorns.
Among New England hawthorns, fanleaf hawthorn is distinguished by its broader, more fan-shaped leaves compared to most relatives.
Among New England hawthorns, Biltmore hawthorn stands out for its green, yellow, or orange fruits - most others like dotted hawthorn, common hawthorn, and cockspur hawthorn have red fruits.

Cleft-leaved hawthorn's leaves are much more deeply divided than most New England hawthorns - while dotted hawthorn has shallow lobes and cockspur hawthorn has barely any lobes at all, this species' leaves are cut nearly to the midrib.

Among New England's hawthorns, pea hawthorn stands out for having the smallest fruits in the genus - significantly smaller than the cherry-sized fruits of dotted hawthorn or the larger berries of cockspur hawthorn.
Blanchard's hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having more deeply lobed leaves and longer thorns.
Miss Jones' hawthorn is distinguished from other New England hawthorns primarily by subtle differences in leaf shape, thorn characteristics, and fruit details that require close examination.
Stone's hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having more deeply lobed leaves and different fruit characteristics.
Fleshy hawthorn stands out from its many hawthorn relatives by having the juiciest, most succulent berries in the group.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, scarlet hawthorn is distinguished by its particularly prominent thorns and bright red fruits.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, Schuette's hawthorn is distinguished by subtle characteristics that require expert identification.
Northern hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having less deeply lobed leaves and different fruit characteristics, though these distinctions can be subtle.
Dodge's hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having less prominently marked leaves and typically fewer, larger thorns.
Holmes' hawthorn is most closely related to scarlet hawthorn but distinguished by its more elongated leaves and egg-shaped rather than round fruits.
Among New England's many hawthorns, broad-leaved cockspurthorn stands out for its exceptionally broad, substantial leaves that are wider than most of its relatives.
Hairy cockspurthorn differs from its closest relative, downy hawthorn, primarily in having about 10 stamens per flower instead of 20, and the two species have separate native ranges.

Grove hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having longer thorns and less deeply cut leaves.
Keep's Hawthorn differs from common hawthorns like dotted hawthorn in subtle leaf lobe patterns and fruit characteristics that require expert knowledge to distinguish reliably.

Among New England hawthorns, poplar hawthorn stands out immediately for its broad, oval, relatively unlobed leaves - most other hawthorns like dotted hawthorn or common hawthorn have deeply cut, lobed leaves.
Unlike the common red-fruited hawthorns like dotted hawthorn or cockspur hawthorn, straw-fruited hawthorn produces distinctively pale yellow berries.

Among New England's many hawthorn species, stinking hawthorn stands out for its yellow-green fruits with red markings rather than the solid red fruits of most others like dotted hawthorn or cockspur hawthorn.
